items.why: Arch gives 3 branches; lies posterior to manubrium; L vagus crosses it, L RLN loops under it.

questions.q: Which nerve loops under the aortic arch?
questions.explain: The left vagus crosses anterior to the aortic arch and gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops under the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.q: In the superior mediastinum, the aortic arch and its branches lie in what position relative to the sternum (manubrium)?
questions.explain: The aortic arch and its branches are positioned posterior to the sternum, deep to the manubrium, above the sternal angle.

items.why: First arch branch; divides into R common carotid + R subclavian.

questions.q: The brachiocephalic trunk divides into which two arteries?
choices: Right and left common carotid arteries
Right subclavian and right internal thoracic
Right common carotid and right vertebral
Right common carotid and right subclavian
questions.explain: The brachiocephalic artery divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries, supplying the right head, neck and right upper limb.

items.why: Branch of brachiocephalic trunk; right head and neck.

questions.q: The right common carotid artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explain: Unlike the left common carotid (a direct arch branch), the right common carotid comes off the brachiocephalic trunk.

items.why: Branch of brachiocephalic trunk; R RLN hooks under it; right upper limb.

questions.q: What does the right subclavian artery primarily supply?
choices: Right side of the head and neck
questions.explain: The brachiocephalic trunk's right subclavian branch supplies the right upper limb; the right common carotid supplies the right head and neck.

items.why: Direct arch branch; left head and neck; L phrenic descends between it and L subclavian.

questions.q: Which region does the left common carotid artery supply?
choices: Right side of the head and neck
Left side of the head and neck
questions.explain: The left common carotid artery is the second arch branch and supplies the left side of the head and neck.

questions.q: Which nerve descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries?
questions.explain: The left phrenic nerve descends between the left subclavian and left common carotid arteries, then crosses the left side of the arch anterior to the left vagus.

items.why: Third arch branch; left upper limb.

questions.q: The left subclavian artery mainly supplies which region?
choices: Left side of the head and neck
questions.explain: The left subclavian artery, the third branch of the aortic arch, supplies the left upper limb.

items.why: Formed by R + L brachiocephalic veins; drains upper body to RA; SVC syndrome.

questions.q: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of which veins?
choices: Right and left internal jugular veins
questions.explain: The SVC is formed by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins and drains the upper body into the right atrium.

questions.q: A mass in the superior mediastinum compresses the SVC. Which presentation is most expected?
choices: Leg swelling and distended abdominal veins
Facial swelling and distended chest veins
questions.explain: SVC syndrome raises upper-body venous pressure: facial and neck swelling, distended chest wall veins, and a widened mediastinum on imaging.

items.why: Unite to form SVC; drain head, neck, upper limbs.

questions.q: The brachiocephalic veins drain blood from which regions?
questions.explain: Brachio = arm, cephalic = head: the brachiocephalic veins drain the head, neck and upper limbs and join to form the SVC.

items.why: Drains right posterior thoracic wall into the SVC.

questions.q: The azygos vein empties into which vessel?
questions.explain: The azygos vein drains the right posterior thoracic wall and arches forward to empty into the SVC.

items.why: Parasympathetic to heart/lungs; R vagus behind SVC + R bronchus; L vagus anterior to arch; medial to phrenic.

questions.q: Vagal (parasympathetic) input to the heart has what effect?
questions.explain: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart (slows heart rate) and lungs (bronchoconstriction).

questions.q: Compared with the phrenic nerves, where do the vagus nerves lie in the superior mediastinum?
questions.explain: The vagus nerves are more medial because they head into the middle mediastinum to innervate the heart, airways and esophagus; the phrenic nerves stay lateral on the pericardial sac.

questions.q: The right vagus nerve runs posterior to which structures?
questions.explain: The right vagus runs posterior to the SVC and right primary bronchus; the left vagus crosses anterior to the aortic arch.

items.why: Branch of R vagus; hooks under R subclavian; supplies larynx; injury -> hoarseness.

questions.q: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under which artery?
questions.explain: The right RLN wraps under the right subclavian artery, while the left RLN loops under the aortic arch.

questions.q: A patient develops new hoarseness after a thyroidectomy. Injury to this nerve best explains it because it supplies...
questions.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply most of the muscles of the larynx, controlling the vocal cords; injury paralyzes a cord and causes a hoarse voice.

items.why: Branch of L vagus; loops under arch at ligamentum arteriosum; PDA ligation / tumor -> hoarseness.

questions.q: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch next to which structure?
questions.explain: The left RLN passes under the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum, which is why PDA ligation can injure it.

questions.q: A lung tumor invading the region beneath the aortic arch causes a hoarse voice. Which other nerve injury could produce the same deficit?
choices: Left vagus nerve above its RLN branch
Left phrenic nerve near the pericardium
questions.explain: Injury to a vagus nerve proximal to its recurrent laryngeal branch has the same effect as RLN injury: vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.

items.why: C3-C5; anterior to lung root along lateral pericardium; motor to diaphragm, sensory to pericardium.

questions.q: From which spinal nerve roots does the phrenic nerve arise?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5; injury above this level paralyzes the diaphragm and prevents spontaneous breathing.

questions.q: Below the superior mediastinum, the phrenic nerves descend in what relation to the lung root?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerves descend anterior to the root of the lungs along the lateral fibrous pericardium; the vagus nerves pass posterior to the lung root.

questions.q: Besides motor supply to the diaphragm, the phrenic nerves carry sensory fibers from which structure?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerves provide sensory innervation to the pericardium and to the peritoneum on the underside of the diaphragm.

items.why: Anterior to esophagus in superior mediastinum; tumor compression -> cough.

questions.q: In the superior mediastinum, the trachea lies in what relation to the esophagus?
questions.explain: The trachea lies anterior to the esophagus, which rests in the groove of the posterior trachea.

items.why: Rests in the posterior tracheal groove; passes into posterior mediastinum.
Remnant of ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk to aorta); PDA -> L-to-R shunt.

questions.q: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of which fetal structure?
questions.explain: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which normally closes after birth.

questions.q: A patent ductus arteriosus produces which type of shunt?
questions.explain: A PDA connects the aorta to the pulmonary artery, creating a left-to-right shunt that increases pulmonary blood flow and risks heart failure.

items.why: Landmark: anterior mediastinum lies anterior to the sac, posterior mediastinum posterior to it.

questions.q: The posterior mediastinum is defined as the region posterior to which structure?
questions.explain: The anterior mediastinum lies anterior to the pericardial sac and the posterior mediastinum lies posterior to it.

items.why: Posterior mediastinum; gives posterior intercostal arteries; lies posterior to esophagus.

questions.q: The descending (thoracic) aorta gives rise to which arteries?
questions.explain: The descending aorta is the thoracic portion of the aorta in the posterior mediastinum and gives rise to the posterior intercostal arteries.

questions.q: Which structure lies posterior to the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum?
questions.explain: The descending aorta is posterior to the esophagus; the heart (left atrium), thymus and bronchi are anterior to it.

questions.q: A patient with chronic dysphagia has a barium swallow showing extrinsic narrowing of the thoracic esophagus. Which vascular lesion is a recognized cause?
questions.explain: Although uncommon, a thoracic aortic aneurysm can compress the esophagus and cause abnormal narrowing and chronic dysphagia.

items.why: Azygos system drains thoracic wall; alternative pathway to IVC; thoracic duct lies between azygos and esophagus.

questions.q: The azygos system can serve as an alternative venous pathway for which vessel?
questions.explain: The azygos, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins drain the thoracic wall and can function as an alternative pathway to the IVC.

questions.q: During ligation for chylothorax, the surgeon finds the thoracic duct between the azygos vein and which structure?
questions.explain: The thoracic duct (the 'duck between two gooses') lies between the azygos vein and esophagus, with the aorta posterior.

items.why: Part of azygos system; drains thoracic wall.

questions.q: The accessory hemiazygos vein receives venous blood mainly from which region?
questions.explain: The azygos system (azygos, accessory hemiazygos and hemiazygos veins) receives venous blood from the thoracic wall.

items.why: Part of azygos system; drains thoracic wall.
Ganglionated chain beside vertebral column; fight-or-flight.

questions.q: Which best describes the thoracic sympathetic trunk?
choices: Plexus wrapping around the aortic arch
Cranial nerve trunk on the esophagus
questions.explain: The thoracic sympathetic trunk is a ganglionated chain on each side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum.

questions.q: Activation of the sympathetic trunk would be expected to cause which change?
questions.explain: The sympathetic trunk drives the fight-or-flight response, regulating heart rate, blood pressure and digestion (raising heart rate, slowing digestion).

items.why: From T5-T9 ganglia; preganglionic sympathetics through diaphragm to preaortic ganglia.

questions.q: The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve originates from which sympathetic ganglia?
questions.explain: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the medial branches of the 5th-9th thoracic sympathetic ganglia; the lesser arises from T10-T11.

questions.q: Which fiber type does the greater splanchnic nerve carry into the abdomen?
questions.explain: Thoracic splanchnic nerves carry presynaptic (preganglionic) sympathetic fibers from the sympathetic trunk into the abdomen.

questions.q: After traversing the diaphragm, the greater splanchnic nerve synapses in which ganglia?
questions.explain: The splanchnic nerves pass through the diaphragm to reach the preaortic (prevertebral) ganglia for sympathetic innervation of abdominal structures.

items.why: Posterior to LA, anterior to vertebrae; constrictions at aortic arch, L main bronchus, diaphragm.

questions.q: The thoracic esophagus lies directly posterior to which heart chamber?
questions.explain: The esophagus courses vertically directly posterior to the left atrium and anterior to the vertebral column.

questions.q: On barium swallow, which three structures normally indent the thoracic esophagus?
choices: Aortic arch, right main bronchus, diaphragm
Azygos arch, left main bronchus, diaphragm
Aortic arch, left main bronchus, pericardium
Aortic arch, left main bronchus, diaphragm
questions.explain: The thoracic esophagus is compressed by the arch of the aorta, the left main bronchus and the diaphragm; these impressions appear as it fills.

items.why: Receives SVC, IVC, coronary sinus; forms right border of cardiac silhouette.

questions.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?
questions.explain: The superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus all drain deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.

questions.q: On a PA chest X-ray, the right atrium forms which part of the cardiac silhouette?
questions.explain: The right atrium is the rightmost part of the heart and forms the right border of the cardiac silhouette.

items.why: Forms most of anterior surface; 1/3 of diaphragmatic surface; most injured in penetrating trauma.

questions.q: A patient has a stab wound just left of the sternum. The right ventricle is the chamber most likely injured because it forms...
choices: The right border of the heart
questions.explain: The RV forms most of the anterior heart and touches the rib cage, making it the chamber most commonly injured in penetrating trauma.

questions.q: What fraction of the diaphragmatic surface of the heart does the right ventricle cover?
questions.explain: The RV covers about one-third of the diaphragmatic surface; the LV forms the remaining two-thirds.

items.why: Receives pulmonary veins; most posterior chamber, abuts esophagus; enlarged in mitral stenosis.

questions.q: A 43-year-old woman with mitral stenosis has dysphagia and hoarseness. Barium swallow shows the esophagus indented from outside. Which chamber is responsible?
questions.explain: Mitral stenosis raises LA pressure and enlarges the left atrium, the most posterior chamber, which presses on the esophagus (Ortner's syndrome).

questions.q: The left atrium receives blood from which vessels?
questions.explain: The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.why: Pumps oxygenated blood to aorta; forms apex, left border, 2/3 of diaphragmatic surface.

questions.q: On a PA chest X-ray, the left ventricle forms which border of the cardiac silhouette?
questions.explain: The left ventricle forms the left border of the cardiac silhouette; the right atrium forms the right border.

questions.q: What fraction of the heart's diaphragmatic surface does the left ventricle form?
questions.explain: The LV forms the apex and about two-thirds of the diaphragmatic border; the RV covers the other third.

items.why: Right AV valve, three leaflets, separates RA from RV.

questions.q: The tricuspid valve separates which two compartments?
questions.explain: The tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve has three leaflets and separates the RA from the RV.

items.why: Semilunar valve; outflow of RV to pulmonary circulation.

questions.q: The pulmonary valve separates the right ventricle from which structure?
questions.explain: The pulmonary valve is the semilunar valve in the RV outflow tract, separating the RV from the pulmonary circulation.

items.why: Left AV (bicuspid) valve; two leaflets; separates LA from LV; stenosis -> LA enlargement.

questions.q: How many leaflets does the mitral valve normally have?
questions.explain: The mitral (bicuspid) valve on the left has two leaflets; the tricuspid on the right has three.

questions.q: Mitral stenosis directly increases pressure in which chamber?
questions.explain: The mitral valve separates the LA from the LV; stenosis raises LA pressure and leads to LA enlargement.

items.why: Semilunar valve between LV and aorta; normally three leaflets.

questions.q: The aortic valve separates which two structures?
questions.explain: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve in the LV outflow tract, separating the LV from the aorta.

items.why: Separates the ventricles; membranous + muscular parts.

questions.q: The interventricular septum consists of which two portions?
questions.explain: The interventricular septum separates the two ventricles and has a membranous portion and a muscular portion.

items.why: In interatrial septum; remnant of foramen ovale.

questions.q: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of which embryologic structure?
questions.explain: The fossa ovalis, in the interatrial septum between the RA and LA, is a remnant of the embryologic foramen ovale.

items.why: Parallel myocardial ridges in RA; improve contraction efficiency without much mass.

questions.q: Where are the pectinate muscles described in this brick found?
questions.explain: Pectinate muscles are parallel ridges of myocardium in the right atrium, anterior to the crista terminalis.

questions.q: What is the main function of the pectinate muscles?
choices: Anchor the AV valve leaflets during systole
Carry the right bundle branch onward
Boost contraction without adding much mass
Insulate the atria from the ventricles
questions.explain: Pectinate muscles increase atrial contraction efficiency without adding significant mass.

items.why: Ridge separating smooth posterior RA from pectinate region; landmark for SA node.

questions.q: The crista terminalis is a surface landmark for which structure?
questions.explain: The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the RA that serves as a landmark for the SA node.

questions.q: The crista terminalis separates which two regions?
questions.explain: It separates the smooth posterior wall of the RA from the rough region lined with pectinate muscles.

items.why: Collects most cardiac venous blood; opens into RA near tricuspid valve.

questions.q: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near which valve?
questions.explain: The coronary sinus collects most cardiac venous blood and drains into the RA near the tricuspid valve.

items.why: RV muscular band carrying part of right bundle branch to anterior papillary muscle.

questions.q: What does the septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) carry?
choices: Part of the right bundle branch
Part of the left bundle branch
questions.explain: The moderator band is a muscular band in the RV that carries part of the right bundle branch, aiding coordinated contraction.

questions.q: The moderator band runs to which papillary muscle?
choices: Posterior papillary muscle of the RV
Septal papillary muscle of the LV
Anterior papillary muscle of the RV
Posteromedial papillary muscle of the LV
questions.explain: The septomarginal trabecula carries conduction fibers to the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle.

items.why: AV valve leaflets open in diastole, held closed in systole by chordae/papillary tension.

questions.q: During ventricular diastole, what is the state of the AV valve leaflets and the semilunar valves?
questions.explain: In diastole the AV valves open to let the ventricles fill from the atria while the semilunar valves stay shut.

items.why: Semilunar valves have three overlapping leaflets; no chordae.

questions.q: Semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae. What prevents their leaflets from prolapsing?
questions.explain: Although semilunar valves lack chordae and papillary muscles, the overlap of each valve's three leaflets prevents prolapse.

items.why: Fibrous cords connecting AV valves to papillary muscles; tense in systole.

questions.q: The chordae tendineae connect the AV valve cusps to which structures?
questions.explain: The chordae tendineae are fibrous cords in the ventricles that connect the AV valves to the papillary muscles.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, what is the state of the chordae tendineae?
questions.explain: In systole the papillary muscles tension the chordae, which keeps the AV valves from prolapsing into the atria.

items.why: Anchor chordae; rupture 2-7 days post-MI -> acute mitral regurgitation.

questions.q: Four days after an MI, a patient develops sudden heart failure and a new murmur from papillary muscle rupture. Which valve lesion results?
questions.explain: Papillary muscle rupture (2-7 days post-MI) can cause complete mitral valve insufficiency/regurgitation, a surgical emergency.

questions.q: Contraction of the papillary muscles during systole serves to...
questions.explain: When the ventricles contract, papillary muscles tension the chordae tendineae so the AV valves don't prolapse into the atria.

items.why: Irregular muscular ridges lining ventricles; reduce suction.

questions.q: What is the function of the trabeculae carneae?
choices: Anchor AV valve cusps during systole
Insulate the atria from the ventricles
Mark the location of the SA node
questions.explain: Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges lining the ventricles that help prevent suction during contraction by reducing smooth surfaces.

items.why: Ear-shaped atrial appendages; LA auricle common thrombus site in AF.

questions.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has an embolic stroke. Where did the thrombus most likely form?
questions.explain: The left atrial auricle is a common site of thrombus in atrial fibrillation due to blood stasis; dislodged clots cause embolic strokes.

items.why: Delivers deoxygenated upper-body blood into RA.
Delivers deoxygenated lower-body blood into RA.

questions.q: The inferior vena cava drains the lower body into which chamber?
questions.explain: The SVC and IVC deliver deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation into the right atrium.

items.why: Formed by the left atrium; trachea lies superior to it.

questions.q: Which chamber forms the base of the heart?
questions.explain: The left atrium forms the base and the most posterior region of the heart.

items.why: Formed by LV; points downward, forward and to the left.

questions.q: Which chamber forms the apex of the heart?
questions.explain: The left ventricle forms the apex, the most inferior and leftward point of the heart.

questions.q: In which direction does the apex of the heart point?
questions.explain: The apex points downward, forward and to the left; about two-thirds of the heart lies left of midline.

items.why: Carries deoxygenated blood from RV to lungs.
Only major arteries carrying deoxygenated blood.

questions.q: Unlike most arteries, the pulmonary arteries carry which type of blood?
questions.explain: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the RV to the lungs and are the only major arteries that do so.

items.why: Return oxygenated blood from lungs to LA.

questions.q: The pulmonary veins carry what kind of blood to which chamber?
questions.explain: The pulmonary veins deliver oxygenated blood from the lungs back into the left atrium.

items.why: Pericardial effusion: rounded enlarged silhouette, tamponade impairs filling.

questions.q: A large pericardial effusion causes cardiac tamponade. What does tamponade primarily impair?
questions.explain: Tamponade is a pericardial effusion compressing the heart, impairing its ability to fill with blood and reducing cardiac output.

items.why: Lies superior to the heart base; cardiomegaly widens the carinal angle.

questions.q: On chest X-ray, marked cardiomegaly pushes into the tracheal bifurcation. What change is seen?
choices: Carina displaced to the left neck
questions.explain: An enlarged heart can push into the tracheal bifurcation, increasing the angle between the right and left bronchi.

bricks.title: Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Heart

items.why: Coronaries arise just distal to the aortic valve; aortic stenosis -> angina.

questions.q: Why can aortic stenosis cause angina?
choices: The coronaries arise from the pulmonary trunk
The coronaries arise just proximal to the valve
The coronaries arise from the arch branches
The coronaries arise just distal to the valve
questions.explain: Because the coronary arteries emerge from the aorta just distal to the aortic valve, aortic stenosis limits coronary as well as peripheral flow.

items.why: Left main: courses behind pulmonary trunk; splits into LAD + LCX; supplies LA, LV, most of septum; fills in diastole.

questions.q: The left coronary artery divides into which two branches?
questions.explain: The LCA courses behind the pulmonary trunk and divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCX) arteries.

questions.q: The left coronary artery courses behind which structure before dividing?
questions.explain: The LCA passes behind the pulmonary trunk and then splits into the LAD and LCX.

questions.q: During which phase do the coronary arteries receive most of their blood flow?
questions.explain: During systole the coronaries are compressed; when the LV relaxes in diastole, backflow from the aorta fills the coronary arteries.

items.why: Anterior IV groove to apex; anterior LV, anterolateral papillary, anterior 2/3 of septum; diagonals.

questions.q: Which portion of the interventricular septum does the LAD supply?
questions.explain: The LAD supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum; the PDA supplies the posterior one-third.

questions.q: In which groove does the LAD travel?
questions.explain: The LAD (anterior interventricular artery) runs in the anterior interventricular groove, typically to the apex.

questions.q: Which papillary muscle is supplied by the LAD?
questions.explain: The LAD supplies the anterolateral papillary muscle; the PDA supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle of the LV.

items.why: Runs between LA and LV; supplies LA and posterior/lateral LV (obtuse marginal); gives PDA in left dominance.

questions.q: A 59-year-old man has a severe occlusion of his left circumflex artery. Which structure is most deprived of oxygen?
questions.explain: The LCX travels posteriorly between the LA and LV to supply the left atrium and left ventricle.

questions.q: In a left-dominant circulation, the left circumflex gives rise to which artery?
questions.explain: In left dominance the LCX gives rise to the PDA, so an LCX occlusion puts more myocardium at risk.

items.why: Between SVC/RA and pulmonary trunk in RA-RV groove; SA nodal branch; usually gives PDA.

questions.q: In most people, the SA node is supplied by a branch of which artery?
questions.explain: The SA nodal branch arises near the origin of the RCA; in some variants LCX branches supply the SA node instead.

questions.q: After leaving the aorta, the right coronary artery first passes between which structures?
questions.explain: The RCA first passes between the SVC and pulmonary trunk, then runs between the RA and RV toward the back of the heart.

items.why: RCA branch along lateral margin of RV; supplies RV and apex; accompanied by small cardiac vein.

questions.q: What does the right (acute) marginal artery supply?
questions.explain: The right acute marginal artery runs along the lateral margin of the RV and supplies the RV and the apex.

items.why: Usually from RCA (~85% right dominant); posterior IV groove; AV node, posterior 1/3 septum, inferior wall.

questions.q: In about 85% of people, the posterior descending artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explain: Most people (~85%) are right-dominant, meaning the PDA is a branch of the RCA.

questions.q: Which conduction structure does the posterior descending artery supply?
questions.explain: The PDA supplies the AV node, the posterior one-third of the septum, the inferior wall and the posteromedial papillary muscle.

questions.q: Compared with a right-dominant patient, a left-dominant patient with a left coronary occlusion has more myocardium at risk in which region?
choices: Anterior free wall of the RV
questions.explain: In left dominance the PDA territory (posterior LV and posterior septum) also depends on the left system, so left occlusions put more myocardium at risk.

items.why: Houses bundle of His/bundle branches; perfused by LAD and PDA septal perforators.

questions.q: Occlusion of which pair of arteries can damage the conduction system in the interventricular septum?
questions.explain: The bundle of His and bundle branches lie in the septum, which is perfused by septal perforators of the LAD and PDA.

items.why: Anterolateral (LAD) vs posteromedial (PDA) papillary muscles.

questions.q: The posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle is supplied by which artery?
questions.explain: The PDA supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle; the LAD supplies the anterolateral papillary muscle.

items.why: Receives great, middle, small cardiac veins in posterior coronary sulcus; empties into RA.

questions.q: The coronary sinus empties directly into which chamber?
questions.explain: The coronary sinus empties directly into the RA, alongside the SVC and IVC.

questions.q: Where is the coronary sinus located?
questions.explain: The great, middle and small cardiac veins coalesce into the coronary sinus at the back of the heart within the coronary sulcus.

items.why: Starts at apex, runs with LAD in anterior IV groove, then with LCX in coronary sulcus to coronary sinus.

questions.q: Which artery does the great cardiac vein accompany in the anterior interventricular groove?
questions.explain: The great cardiac vein starts at the apex and runs in the anterior interventricular groove with the LAD, then with the LCX in the coronary sulcus.

items.why: Ascends posterior IV groove with PDA to coronary sinus.

questions.q: The middle cardiac vein runs alongside which artery?
questions.explain: The middle cardiac vein ascends the posterior interventricular groove alongside the PDA before draining into the coronary sinus.

items.why: Accompanies acute marginal artery; right posterior AV groove to coronary sinus.

questions.q: Which cardiac vein accompanies a branch of the right coronary artery along the right margin of the heart?
questions.explain: The small cardiac vein accompanies the acute marginal artery from the RCA, then runs in the right posterior AV groove to the coronary sinus.

questions.q: Before draining into the coronary sinus, the small cardiac vein courses in which groove?
questions.explain: The small cardiac vein courses in the right posterior atrioventricular groove and drains into the coronary sinus.
